source.title: Dropout can create a privileged basis in the ReLU output model.

record.tranche_reason: The post tests superposition-related behavior in a toy ReLU output model using dropout sweeps and measures different from neuron-meaning visualizations.
record.gate_note: The text reports qualitative outcomes for basis orientation and superposition. Plots are described but their numerical values are not present in the supplied text. Cited results and comment-only claims are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The post studies a toy ReLU output model with no privileged basis. It measures whether dropout aligns the hidden basis with coordinate axes, and how dropout changes superposition (WTW, dimensions per feature). It never measures whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated features. Superposition and basis alignment are related constructs, not neuron polysemanticity. So no version is tested, including V3 (causation) and V5 (polysemantic share under regularization). The findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The author concludes that dropout can induce a privileged basis in the rotation-invariant ReLU output model, with distinct regimes by dropout rate and weaker effects for dense features. The author also tentatively concludes that dropout generally inhibits superposition, with exceptions, and that this is hard to quantify.
record.recipe_differences: A toy ReLU output model with dropout-rate sweeps; it measures basis orientation and dimensions per feature rather than visualizing responses of individual trained vision-model neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: The basis-orientation effect differs with dropout rate and feature density; alignment is reported above roughly 50% dropout and is weaker or absent with dense features. Superposition trends vary with dropout and feature sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: In the 2D and higher-dimensional ReLU output model with sparse features, dropout breaks rotational symmetry. Low dropout biases orientation away from the coordinate basis; above ~50% dropout the weights align with the coordinate axes. The effect is much weaker or absent with dense features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout can create a privileged, axis-aligned basis in otherwise rotation-invariant toy models, depending on dropout rate and feature sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: Dropout qualitatively changes learned superposition (WTW). Higher dropout generally gives higher dimensions per feature at a given sparsity, but at low dropout and some sparsities dimensions per feature can be lower.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout generally inhibits superposition in toy models, though not strictly at all dropout and sparsity settings.

record.problems: The evidence is presented qualitatively and the plotted numerical values are not included in the supplied text. The study uses a simplified toy model, and the author says the superposition effect is difficult to quantify and not strict.

untested.parts: Image-classifier neurons; no vision models studied.
Transformer LM MLP neurons; no language models studied.
Whether neurons are polysemantic because of superposition; neuron-level responses are never measured.
Polysemanticity without capacity pressure; all models have n>>m.
Share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures or regularization, and the performance cost; dropout's effect is measured only on superposition and basis alignment.
Dependence of polysemanticity judgments on activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 'supports' label is dropped. Showing superposition exists in a toy model with n>>m, and that dropout reduces it, does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition. No neuron-level polysemanticity is measured, and without dropout the hidden basis has no privileged neurons. Evidence is qualitative only; the figures' values are not in the text. The kurtosis evidence appears only in a commenter's remark and is not a study result.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and responses to image inputs.
Transformer language-model MLP neurons and token or context responses.
The study measures superposition in a toy ReLU output model, but does not directly measure semantic polysemanticity in trained networks or compare capacity-pressure levels to test causation.
Whether polysemanticity arises from initialization, regularization or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
The share of polysemantic neurons, comparisons across architectures or activation functions, and whether it can be lowered without substantial performance loss.
Whether canonical mixed-response neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs.
Whether polysemanticity judgments change with activation range or explanation scoring.
